SUMMARY 
This report recommends that City Council state its intention to designate the property at 
19 Don Ridge Drive under Part IV, Section 29 of the Ontario Heritage Act for its cultural 
heritage value according to the Statement of Significance which includes a description 
of heritage attributes found in Attachment 1. 
The subject property at 19 Don Ridge Drive, known as St. John's York Mills Anglican 
Church, an active Place of Worship, is located on the west side of Yonge Street, north 
of York Mills Road, within the York Mills neighbourhood of North York. The property also 
includes several structures related to the church, including the Lodge (Napier Simpson, 
1958); the Dawson Lychgate, the Kay Gate, and burial grounds. The 1844 church has 
been the subject of additions since construction, including the Parish Hall and 
Auditorium (1939, 1949), and the McCollum Wing (1968). The focus of this report is the 
original 1844 church structure, not any of its later additions, auxiliary structures, or the 
adjacent burial grounds. 
A location map and current photograph of the heritage property are included in 
Attachment 2. 
The property known as St. John’s York Mills Anglican Church is a buff brick Gothic 
Revival church reflective of the work of the architect John George Howard and his 
application of a restrained Gothic style to ecclesiastical commissions through the 1840s 
in Upper Canada. Built as the second iteration of St. John’s York Mills Anglican Church, 
the present structure comprises the original 1844 church with additions from 1939, 
1949, and 1968. The primary (west) façade faces southwest towards Yonge Street, and 
while largely obscured by mature trees today, was at one time highly visible from the 
valley below. While the 1844 church has been the subject of extensive additions and 
alterations, the integrity of John Howard’s Gothic Revival design remains intact and 
visible from each elevation. The additions have been designed using complementary

materials, and have not subsumed the church in their scale, form, or massing, ensuring 
the legibility of the 1844 church from various perspectives and vantage points. 
The congregation of St John’s York Mills Anglican Church traces its history back to the 
establishment of the Town of York in 1793, and the arrival of United Empire Loyalists to 
York soon after. Originally founded in 1816, the church and its original parishioners, 
many of whom are interred on the grounds, have deep roots within York Mills. 
Today, though much of York Mills' rural character has been replaced by suburban 
development, there remain several area heritage properties that share a similar period 
of construction with St. John’s York Mills Anglican Church. These include the C.W. 
Jefferys House (1833; Part IV) at 4111 Yonge Street, the John Street Worker's Cottages 
(1860; Listed) at 4150 Yonge Street, St. John's Rectory (1878; Part IV) at 174 Old 
Yonge Street, the York Mills Baptist Church Manse (1850, Listed) at 106 York Mills 
Road, and the Jolly Miller Tavern (1857; Part IV) at 3885 Yonge Street. Collectively, and 
alongside the remaining natural features including the ridge and western branch of the 
Don River, these properties convey the history of colonial settlement and religious 
practice within York Mills through the nineteenth and into the twentieth centuries and 
are valued by the present-day community of York Mills and North York. 
The subject property at 19 Don Ridge Drive was listed on the City of Toronto's Heritage 
Register on September 27, 2006. 
This property is one of eighteen pre-1870 listed properties citywide which have been 
identified as candidates for designation through the City's implementation of Bill 23 
amendments to the Ontario Heritage Act and its ongoing prioritization strategy for listed 
properties that must be designated or removed from the Heritage Register by January 
1, 2027. 
Part of the strategy for the review of listed properties on the Heritage Register includes 
the procurement of qualified heritage consultants to research, evaluate, and prepare 
heritage evaluation reports for a subset of listed properties prioritized for designation. 
City Planning retained the services of Alex Corey Heritage Consulting ("the Consultant") 
to research and evaluate a citywide group of eighteen pre-1870 listed properties which 
includes the subject property at 19 Don Ridge Drive. The Consultant evaluated the 
subject property and determined that it meets the provincial criteria. 
The Consultant's research on the subject property is included in Attachment 3 of this 
report. The research, analysis, and evaluation contained within Attachment 3 reflect the 
Consultant's professional expertise and opinion. Staff have independently reviewed the

In accordance with 3.1.6.50 of the Official Plan and the City's Protocol for the

planning, contributing to a sense of place, economic prosperity, and healthy and 
equitable communities. Heritage conservation in Ontario is identified as a provincial 
interest under the Planning Act. https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90p13

the Ontario Heritage Act as the primary legislation through which heritage evaluation 
and heritage conservation will be implemented.

under Part IV, Section 29 of the Ontario Heritage Act. The criteria are based on an 
evaluation of design/physical value, historical and associative value and contextual 
value.  A property may be designated under Section 29 of the Act if it meets two or 
more of the provincial criteria for determining whether it is of cultural heritage value or 
interest.

The property at 19 Don Ridge Drive is worthy of designation under Part IV, Section 29

Description 
The subject property at 19 Don Ridge Drive is located on the west side of Yonge Street, 
north of York Mills Road, within the York Mills neighbourhood of North York. 
Constructed in 1844, the property contains St. John’s York Mills Anglican Church, an 
active Place of Worship. The property also includes several structures related to the 
church, including the Lodge (Napier Simpson, 1958); the Dawson Lychgate, the Kay 
Gate, and burial grounds. The 1844 church has been the subject of additions since 
construction, including the Parish Hall and Auditorium (1939, 1949), and the McCollum 
Wing (1968). The focus of this report is the original 1844 church structure, not any of its 
later additions, auxiliary structures, or the adjacent burial grounds. 
Statement of Cultural Heritage Value 
Design or Physical Value 
The property at 19 Don Ridge Drive is a representative example of the Gothic Revival 
style of ecclesiastical architecture employed by the prominent architect John George 
Howard in the design and construction of several churches across Southern Ontario in 
the 1840s. More specifically, it is a representative example of what has been referred to 
as “Commissioners Gothic,” in reference to an Act passed in Britain in 1818 to advance 
funds to the construction of Parish churches and which advocated for designs that 
employed a specific form of Gothic architecture based on Classical arrangements. 
Architecturally, this is represented in the combination of the classically inspired 
rectangular preaching-box layout with Gothic pointed windows and ornamentation, both 
seen at St. John’s York Mills. The conservatively adorned interior gives way to the 
Gothically-inspired exterior, featuring simple buff brick buttresses, lancet and pointed 
arched window and door openings with Gothic tracery, drip moulds, pinnacles, and 
belfry. The subsequent additions (1939, 1949, and 1968) have been designed to be 
contextually appropriate through their materiality and details and subordinate through 
scale, location, form, and massing to the 1844 church, and do not detract from the 
integrity of Howard’s design or its ability to convey the Commissioners Gothic 
architectural style. 
Historical or Associative Value 
The property at 19 Don Ridge Drive has historical value for its direct associations with 
the establishment of the Anglican Church within Upper Canada and the Town of York, 
and with the founding of St. John’s York Mills parish within the community of York Mills. 
Following the founding of the Town of York in 1793 and the construction of Yonge 
Street connecting York to Holland’s Landing, the settlement of York Mills grew along the 
19 Don Ridge Drive - Notice of Intention to Designate Page 7 of 33

banks of the Western branch of the Don River. The growth of the community 
precipitated the need for a mission church to serve the growing congregation that had 
been meeting in residences and a schoolhouse in Hogg’s Hollow. Driven by the support 
of local families, including the Ketchums, Van Nostrands, Marshes, and Sheppards, St. 
John’s Chapel was completed in 1817 and was the first mission of St. James Church, in 
the Town of York. Consecrated in 1829 and declared a Crown Rectory in 1836, the 
current church was constructed in 1844 and consecrated that same year. Celebrating its 
bicentennial in 2016, St John’s York Mills Anglican Church is recognized as the oldest 
parish church within the present-day City of Toronto and retains an active congregation 
that continues to be involved in the social, religious, and educational life of York Mills 
and North York. 
The continued operation of the church as a Place of Worship, with its extensive on-site 
archives and the incorporation of physical elements relating to the former York Mills 
Baptist and Presbyterian Churches, as well as the first St. John’s York Mills Church, has 
the potential to yield information on the early history of the Anglican Church within 
Upper Canada, and the history of the settlement of York Mills. 
St. John’s York Mills Anglican Church has associative value as it reflects the work of the 
architect John George Howard, Toronto’s first professional architect in the mid-
nineteenth century. John Howard was responsible for the design of numerous 
residential, commercial, and institutional buildings throughout Upper Canada, drawing 
inspiration from his upbringing and training in England prior to emigrating to Canada in 
1832. Among his ecclesiastical commissions were several country churches for both the 
Anglican and Catholic diocese where Howard employed a form of Gothic Revival 
termed “Commissioners Gothic,” incorporating classical forms with Gothic 
ornamentation in a formulaic method that could be adapted to different contexts and 
specific church needs. This style is well-represented at St. John’s York Mills Anglican 
Church (1844), as well as his commissions for Christ Church Tyendinaga (1843), Christ 
Church Holland Landing (1843), and St. John’s Anglican Church in Jordan (1841). St. 
John’s York Mills Anglican Church is an important and significant example of John 
Howard’s work with this style within the City of Toronto, and alongside its 
contemporaries illustrates Howard’s approach towards ecclesiastical architecture during 
this period of colonization and expansion within Upper Canada. 
Contextual Value 
The property at 19 Don Ridge Drive has contextual value as it is historically linked to its 
surroundings, which include several properties that share a similar period of 
construction with St. John’s York Mills Anglican Church and that collectively relay the 
history of the community. These include:

• 4150 Yonge Street, John Street Worker’s Cottages (1860, listed) 
• 174 Old Yonge Street, St John’s Rectory (1878, designated Part IV) 
• 106 York Mills Road, York Mills Baptist Church Manse (1850, listed) 
• 3885 Yonge Street, Jolly Miller Tavern (1857, designated Part IV)

Heritage Attributes 
Design and Physical Value 
Attributes that contribute to 19 Don Ridge Drive being a representative example of the 
Commissioners Gothic architectural style: 
• The scale, form, and massing of the 1844 church, situated atop a ridge of land 
overlooking the York Mills valley and the western branch of the Don River 
• The arrangement of the church featuring a central and prominent bell tower, 
standing proud of the main body containing the nave and apse with low-pitched 
sloped roofs on either side 
• The central bell tower, divided into three sections comprising the primary entrance 
at-grade, window openings on the second section, and louvered openings for the 
belfry, crowned by stepped gable crenellations 
• The primary use of buff brick with stone detailing including drip moulds, capstones, 
sills, and finials 
• The Gothic pointed arch window openings on the bell tower, west, north, and south 
facades, containing Gothic tracery 
• The buff brick buttresses on the north and south facades, set between pointed arch 
window openings illuminating the nave within 
• The primary (west) entrance set within the bell tower and composed of wood double 
doors, along with the secondary entrance into the narthex on the south façade with 
wood double doors 
• The rear (east) façade comprised of buff brick cladding punctuated by a pointed arch 
window opening and set below a cast stone cross finial perched at the roof peak 
Historical Value 
Attributes that contribute to 19 Don Ridge Drive having historic value and an association

settlement of York Mills: 
• The date stone surmounting the primary (west) entrance on the bell tower 
• The wood beams inside the narthex of the church, which were originally used in the 
construction of York Mills Baptist Church and the first iteration of St. John’s York 
Mills Anglican Church 
• The eastern Dawson Lychgate, providing access into the churchyard from Old 
Yonge Street 
• The western Kay Gate, providing pedestrian access from Yonge Street up the ridge 
to the primary entrance of the 1844 church

Indigenous Communities 
For time immemorial, Toronto has been home to Indigenous peoples. Ojibway oral 
histories speak of Ice People, who lived at a time when ice covered the land.1 Following 
the retreat of glaciers approximately 13,000 years ago, small groups of Indigenous 
peoples moved from place to place, hunting and gathering the food they needed 
according to the seasons. Over millennia, they adapted to dramatically changing 
environmental conditions, developing and acquiring new technologies as they did 
so. Waterways and the lake were vital sources of fresh water and nourishment, and 
shorelines and nearby areas were important sites for gathering, trading, hunting, fishing, 
and ceremonies. Long-distance trade moved valuable resources across the land. 
After maize and squash were introduced to Southern Ontario, by approximately 500 CE, 
horticulture began to supplement food sources. By 1300 CE, villages focused on 
growing food became year-round settlements surrounded by crops. These villages were 
home to ancestors of the Huron-Wendat Nation, who would continue to occupy 
increasingly larger villages in the Toronto area and beyond. These villages were 
connected to well-established travel routes which were part of local and long-distance 
trail networks, including the Carrying Place trails on the Don, Rouge and Humber rivers 
that connected Lake Ontario to Georgian Bay. Beads made from seashells from the 
eastern seaboard were found at the Alexandra site in North York, which was a 
community of 800-1000 people in approximately 1350. 
By 1600, the Wendat had formed a confederation of individual nations, and had 
concentrated most of their villages away from Lake Ontario, in the Georgian Bay area. 
Following contact with French explorers and missionaries in Southern Ontario in the 
early 1600s, European diseases decimated First Nations. Competition for furs to trade 
with Europeans and the desire to replenish numbers through absorption of captives, 
among other factors,2 contributed to the Beaver Wars, which after 1640, saw the 
Haudenosaunee Confederacy expand into Southern Ontario, dispersing the Wendat. 
Within the boundaries of today's Toronto, the Haudenosaunee Confederacy then 
occupied villages on the Carrying Place trails on the Humber and Rouge Rivers from 
approximately the 1660s to the 1680s. 
In the late 1680s, the Haudenosaunee Confederacy chose to leave their village in the 
Toronto area and returned to their homelands in upstate New York. As evidenced by the 
1701 Great Peace of Montreal, the 1701 Nanfan Treaty, and the Dish with One Spoon 
Treaty, the Haudenosaunee continued to have an interest in the resources of the area. 
Anishinaabe people from the Lake Superior region then moved into the Toronto area. 
While the Wendat and Haudenosaunee people lived in year-round villages surrounded 
by crops, the Anishinaabe people continued to live primarily by seasonally moving 
across the land to hunt, fish and gather resources that were available at a specific time, 
including migrating birds and maple syrup. To the west of Toronto, the Anishinaabe

(Alderville, Curve Lake, Hiawatha and Scugog Island). 
The Mississaugas, Chippewa, the Haudenosaunee, or the Wendat did not traditionally 
regard land as a commodity to be sold. Following the Toronto Purchase, the British 
government quickly set out to survey the land into lots which were either sold or granted 
into private ownership of settlers. In 2010, the Government of Canada settled the 
Toronto Purchase Claim with the Mississaugas of the Credit after agreeing that the 
Mississaugas were originally unfairly compensated. In 2018, the Williams Treaties First 
Nations settled litigation about land surrenders and harvesting rights with the 
Governments of Canada and Ontario.

York Mills 
The historic village of York Mills was established on a western branch of the Don River 
where it was crossed by Yonge Street, an early colonial settlement route that was laid 
out by John Graves Simcoe following the establishment of the Town of York on the 
shores of Lake Ontario to the south. Yonge Street roughly followed a route that was 
shown to Simcoe by Indigenous peoples who had used the route as a portage trail 
connecting Lake Ontario with Lake Simcoe. Construction of Yonge Street began in 1794

The first mill constructed in York Mills was built in 1804, followed by two more mills 
around 1817, and 1844, respectively. Various names were used to refer to the 
unincorporated community prior to a post office being established in 1836 and named 
York Mills.5 
Early settlers in York Mills were primarily Loyalists who emigrated to Upper Canada 
following the American Revolutionary War, and Scottish immigrants. The local economy 
revolved around the three mill sites which processed local lumber and grain for market, 
taking advantage of the natural watercourse as well as the strategic route south to 
market along Yonge Street. Related businesses and institutions, including blacksmiths, 
coopers, a tavern, school, and churches, provided essential services to the local and 
surrounding community. 
The largest and first church within the community was St. John’s York Mills Anglican 
Church, the first outpost of St. James Anglican Church. The York Mills Anglican 
congregation began practicing in 1797 in the home of Seneca Ketchum, a Loyalist and 
prominent settler in York Mills whose family emigrated from New York State. St. John’s 
York Mills first church was completed in 1817, with the present-day church building 
constructed in 1844. The Anglican church was later joined by the Baptist and 
Presbyterian churches, both with smaller congregations, and neither of which remain 
standing today. 
The community of York Mills remained small despite its strategic location along Yonge 
Street and along the western branch of the Don River; in 1870 its recorded population 
stood only at 100, with mills remaining the primary local economic activity. The village 
character prevailed into the twentieth century, with gradual development occurring as 
the City of Toronto expanded northwards; in 1922 the Township of North York was 
carved out from the northern portion of York Township, comprising primarily agricultural 
land interspersed with small villages and settlements, including York Mills. Suburban 
development increased in the post-war period, spurred by government incentives for 
single-family housing construction, the expansion of car ownership and highways, and 
public transportation. The Borough of North York was established in 1967 followed by 
the City of North York in 1979, and in 1998 amalgamation saw the community of York 
Mills incorporated into the City of Toronto. 
Today, the former village of York Mills is an established residential neighbourhood 
characterized by post-war suburban housing and commercial development along Yonge 
Street. While much of the historic village character has been lost, a select few 
properties from the nineteenth century remain, complemented by the unique and varied 
topography that attracted settlement and supported the community’s early development 
and economic activity.

St. John’s York Mills Anglican Church 
The congregation of St John’s York Mills Anglican Church traces its history back to the 
establishment of the Town of York in 1793, and the arrival of United Empire Loyalists to 
York soon after. The first Anglican services within the York Mills community were hosted 
by Seneca Ketchum (1772 – 1850), who arrived in Upper Canada c.1792 and settled in 
the Town of York with his brother, Jesse Ketchum, by 1797.6 
While Jesse Ketchum established strong roots within the Town of York, his older brother 
Seneca focused on the acquisition of land to the north, along Yonge Street south of 
York Mills within the present-day Bedford Park and Teddington Park neighbourhoods.7 
Seneca’s religious fervour was evidenced in his commitment to the small community 
that was growing around York Mills; on Sundays Seneca would travel south to St. 
James Church (built 1807) in the Town of York, returning later that day to read the 
service at his Bedford Park home.8 Once a month, Reverand John Strachan would 
travel to the community to preach or would otherwise send students to read to the 
congregation. As the congregation grew, services were moved to a schoolhouse in 
Hogg’s Hollow on land owned by Thomas Mercer.9 
By 1816, the growing congregation, buoyed by wealth being generated by the mills 
operating along the banks of the western branch of the Don River, agreed to finance the 
construction of a simple chapel, with the endorsement of Lieutenant Governor Gore and 
Reverand John Strachan. The land for the chapel was donated by Joseph and 
Catherine Sheppard on a rise of land overlooking the valley. The cornerstone of the 
chapel was laid on September 17, 1816, by Gore and Strachan for a simple one-room 
chapel of frame construction measuring 30 by 60 feet located east of the present 
structure. When completed in 1817, the chapel was the second Anglican Church within 
the Home District (comprising Northumberland, Durham, York and Simcoe Counties), 
and the first mission of St. James Church. The chapel was subsequently consecrated in 
1829 as St. John’s Church.10 
Construction of the chapel was a community-effort; with little financial support from 
church or state, the Anglican community of York Mills fundraised through subscriptions, 
donations, labour and land.11 Notable families within the community that played a 
significant role in fundraising for the new church included the Van Nostrands, Hoggs, 
Sheppards, Ketchums, Farrs, and Mercers, all of whom are represented within the 
present-day burial grounds. 
The small confines of the one-room chapel, heated only through a simple stove in the 
centre of the hall, were apparent by the 1830s, and no longer reflected the increasingly 
prosperous community nor supported its size. This coincided with St. John’s being 
declared a Crown Rectory in 1836, the allotment of half of St. James’s endowment of 
land to St. John's, and the appointment of the church’s first rector, Reverand Charles

Matthews. In 1842 a building committee was established led by prominent members of 
the congregation who subsequently retained the architect John George Howard (1803 – 
1890) to prepare plans for a new church. 
The cornerstone for the new church was laid on May 30, 1843, with Bishop John 
Strachan once again in attendance, and the new church opened on June 11, 1844. The 
old church was sold to Edward Pearse who relocated it to Yonge and Sheppard for use 
as a shed. In full circle, beams from the old church were returned in 1948 and 
incorporated within the narthex.12 
The second iteration of St. John’s York Mills Anglican Church was built to the west of 
the former church, closer to the ridge overlooking the valley and offering sweeping 
views of Hogg’s Hollow. This location also afforded St. John’s a position where it could 
serve as a prominent and highly visible landmark for travellers along Yonge Street 
heading north to Holland’s Landing from the City of Toronto. Access to the church was 
permitted via a carriageway traversing the steep incline from Yonge Street (on land 
donated in 1857 by William Marsh),13 as well as from the east through the burial 
grounds from Old Yonge Street. The rectory for St. John’s was built immediately south 
of the eastern entrance at the present-day address of 174 Old Yonge Street, which 
remained within the church’s ownership until 2007 and is now a private residence. 
The newly constructed church was designed by Howard in the Gothic Revival style, 
albeit one of the “mildest Gothic flavour”14 that would be acceptable to Upper Canada’s 
staunchly conservative religious and political elite. The restrained Gothic style employed 
at St. John's and other churches designed by Howard has been called "Commissioners 
Gothic," reflecting features advanced by the Church Building Commissioners in England 
as part of the Church Building Act of 1818 and 1824.15 The Act advocated for parish 
churches to be informed by Classically-inspired rectangular preaching-box churches 
with Gothic windows and ornamentation, with the church commissioners perceiving the 
Gothic style to be the most economical means of church architecture requiring “only a 
belfry and lancet windows to distinguish a building as a church.”16 Howard was almost 
certainly aware of the Act, and as an architect with British roots would have likely sought 
to emulate the architecture of England rather than adopting the more purely classical 
ecclesiastical architecture of the United States. 
The interior of St. John’s York Mills was restrained in ornamentation, with a vestibule at 
the west (front) giving way to the central nave, and with the chancel and apse towards 
the east. A gallery, accessed via the vestibule, features the prized barrel organ for 
which the congregation fundraised and had shipped from London, England by T.C. 
Bates & Sons in 1847, as well as the original box pews. The newly constructed church 
was consecrated in 1849.17

The enthusiasm and growth that spurred the construction of the new St. John’s York 
Mills Anglican Church within the community quieted through the 1850s and the second 
half of the nineteenth century; changes in transportation saw commercial traffic along 
Yonge Street shift westwards to new rail lines, and the community remained well-
outside the City of Toronto to see it benefit from suburban residential development until 
the twentieth century. In 1926, the first Parish Hall was constructed, replaced on the eve 
of World War II, in 1939, by the first phase of a new Parish Hall designed by the 
architects Molesworth, Secord, and Savage and extending from the southern façade of 
the main church. 
Hosting over 300 families with a mere 250 seats by the 1940s, the growing 
congregation was in desperate need of more space within the nave, as well as 
additional space to host community events. The upper floors of the Parish Hall, the 
Auditorium and the Children’s Chapel were completed in 1949 and dedicated in 1952. 
This expansion coincided with a period of development as York Mills experienced the 
suburban growth it had been anticipating since the church was completed in 1844. The 
1949 addition incorporated several elements of significance to the congregation and the 
York Mills community: the narthex features wood beams taken from the demolished first 
church of St. John’s, wood beams from the demolished York Mills Baptist Church 
(previously located at 104 York Mills Road), and stones from the demolished York Mills 
Presbyterian Churchyard that were incorporated into the gallery stairway.18 
The lychgate, or roofed gate, that marks the eastern entrance to the churchyard was 
constructed in 1956 and dedicated to Alexander Dawson, a member of the congregation 
who played an instrumental role in the twentieth-century history of the church.19 It was 
accompanied by a smaller pedestrian gate dedicated to William Kay at the foot of the 
ridge that provided pedestrian access from Yonge Street. The two gates, while varying 
in scale, feature stone foundations, a wood structure and tile roofs. Soon after, in 1958, 
the architect Napier Simpson was retained and built the verger’s house, also known as 
The Lodge, to the northwest of the church atop the ridge. 
The second half of the twentieth century saw St. John’s York Mills Anglican Church 
firmly establish itself as a valued landmark within the community of York Mills and the 
City of North York. In 1968 an addition designed by Page and Steele was constructed 
on the north façade providing an expanded entrance to the church from the parking lot, 
alongside offices and multi-purpose rooms which was christened the Arthur C. 
McCollum Wing in memory of McCollum who served as vicar from 1926 to 1947, and 
Rector until his passing in 1960.20 In 1974, the church played host to Princess Anne 
while she was on an informal tour, an important recognition of the church’s long history 
dating back to its establishment as the second Anglican church in the Home District, 
and a marked change from the routine visit to St. James Cathedral by visiting members 
of the Royal family.21

St. John’s York Mills Anglican Church has maintained a significant position within 
Toronto’s Anglican community through to the present-day and is recognized both for its 
long history dating back to the arrival of the Anglican church to the region, and its later 
history serving the community of York Mills. Today, St. John’s continues to serve its 
congregation as well as the broader community, providing religious, educational, and 
social services and opportunities to York Mills and the City of Toronto. 
John George Howard 
The Toronto-based architect John Howard was retained to prepare plans for the design 
and construction of St John's York Mills Anglican Church in 1842, with construction 
substantially completed in 1843. Howard’s ecclesiastical commissions were primarily, 
although not exclusively, Anglican churches outside the City of Toronto. Similar 
commissions to St. John’s York Mills include Christ Church Tyendinaga (1843); Christ 
Church Holland Landing (1843); and St. John’s Anglican Church in Jordan (1841). 
These churches were relatively simple in their design and construction, likely based off 
a formula that permitted Howard to accept many requests during his peak period of 
ecclesiastical commissions in the 1840s. Collectively, these "Commissioners Gothic" 
churches are characterized by a hall plan with gallery and altar within a rectangular 
body, a low-pitched roof and small chancel, lancet windows, and shallow buttresses. 
Born in England in 1803 with the surname "Corby," Howard received his architectural 
training with the London-based architect William Ford before immigrating to Canada in 
1832. With the support of Sir John Colborne, Howard accepted a position as a drawing 
master at Upper Canada College. Howard was appointed the first Surveyor and City 
Engineer for the newly incorporated City of Toronto in 1834. For the next twenty-one 
years, Howard laid out the municipality’s sewage system and networks of roads and 
sidewalks. He also supervised the surveying of building lots, the most extensive of 
which were plans for the expansion and development of the Toronto Harbour and 
Ashbridge’s Bay. While serving the corporation, Howard accepted both public and 
private architectural commissions, including the landmark Provincial Lunatic Asylum 
(later demolished) and extant projects such as St. John’s Anglican Church in York Mills, 
and his High Park residence named Colborne Lodge (now a city-run museum). 
Howard's architectural practice carried over into landscape design as well and included 
the design of St. James Cemetery (1842), an early example of picturesque cemetery 
design. His design for the subdivision of Samuel Peter Jarvis' estate encompassing 
present-day Jarvis Street from Shuter Street to Bloor Street East included generous 
boulevards lined with trees, creating a park-like residential enclave. 
ii.  ARCHITECTURAL DESCRIPTION 
The following section provides an architectural description and analysis related to the 
property which will establish the basis for determining design or physical value of 
Criteria 1, 2 or 3 according to O. Reg. 9/06 Criteria. 
Located at the top of a ridge overlooking York Mills and the intersection of Yonge Street 
and York Mills Road, St. John’s York Mills Anglican Church is a buff brick Gothic 
Revival church reflective of the work of the architect John George Howard and his 
19 Don Ridge Drive - Notice of Intention to Designate Page 20 of 33

application of a restrained Gothic style to ecclesiastical commissions through the 1840s 
in Upper Canada. 
Built as the second iteration of St. John’s York Mills Anglican Church, the present 
church comprises the original 1844 church with additions from 1939, 1949, and 1968. 
The primary (west) façade faces southwest towards Yonge Street, and while largely 
obscured by mature trees today, was at one time highly visible from the valley below. A 
rectilinear bell tower at centre stands proud of the main body of the church, with tall 
lancet windows on the body of the church on either side of the tower. The bell tower 
comprises three sections: the lower or ground level containing a pointed arch double 
door entry set below a drip mould and a date stone bearing “A.D. 1845”; the middle 
section containing diamond-patterned double-lancet leaded glass windows with sills and 
drip moulds; and the top section, or belfry, with pointed arch louvered openings for the 
bell chamber with accompanying drip moulds above. The top of the tower is 
embellished with a stepped gable and is Norman in design. The corners of the tower 
feature buttresses terminating with stone-capped pinnacles. 
The north façade faces towards a greenspace and driveway and encompasses an 
enlarged entrance as part of the 1968 addition. Four bays of the 1844 church remain 
visible and contain pointed arch window openings with Gothic tracery and stained-glass 
windows set between buff brick buttresses. The 1968 McCollum Wing extends from the 
rear fifth bay and incorporates the memorial chapel. This addition was designed by 
architects Page & Steele in a complementary Brutalist style and was built of brick with 
simple brick piers between rectangular window openings on the west façade and 
pointed openings on the north façade. A turret-like entrance with pointed arch openings 
faces the parking lot and driveway and features a covered entryway ornamented with 
brick piers terminating in cast stone pinnacles. 
The south façade has been significantly altered with the addition of the Parish Hall, 
Children’s Chapel, and Auditorium by architects Molesworth, Secord & Savage (1939, 
1949), comprising two storeys atop a raised basement built of brick. The raised 
basement addition protrudes from the south facade of the 1844 church below pointed 
arch window openings with Gothic tracery and stained-glass windows. A wide variety of 
window openings on the 1949 addition reflect the complex interior arrangement of the 
Parish Hall and Children’s Chapel, as well as varying periods of construction. 
The east (rear) façade of the church faces towards the burial grounds and features an 
asymmetrical design with the apse at centre. The rectangular apse of the church 
features a large, pointed arch window with gothic tracery and stained-glass panes below 
a drip mould; a contemporary rectangular stone finial caps the gabled roof above, with 
large stone buttresses on either corner of the apse. The Parish Hall addition wraps the 
corner with a raised single storey on the south façade. 
While the 1844 church has been the subject of extensive additions and alterations, the 
integrity of John Howard’s Gothic Revival design remains intact and visible from each 
elevation. The additions have been designed using complementary materials, and have 
not subsumed the church in their scale, form, or massing, ensuring the legibility of the 
1844 church from various perspectives and vantage points.

iii. CONTEXT 
The following section provides contextual information and analysis related to the 
property which is the basis for determining contextual value of Criteria 7, 8 or 9 
according to O. Reg. 9/06 Criteria. 
The City of Toronto Property Data Map attached (Attachment 2) shows the site of the 
property at 19 Don Ridge Drive. 
Contextually, St. John’s York Mills Anglican Church is located on the edge of a 
residential neighbourhood primarily comprised of mid-century, post-war, and 
contemporary detached residences. The property extends from Yonge Street to the 
west to Old Yonge Street to the east; the western boundary is largely defined by a 
prominent ridge that descends towards Yonge Street and the natural river valley carved 
by the western branch of the Don River. To the north and south are residential dead-
end streets and cul-de-sacs. The church is significantly buffered on all sides by mature 
trees and green spaces. 
The context within which St. John’s York Mills Anglican Church exists today is a post-
war suburban residential landscape, significantly differing in character and appearance 
from the historically rural context within which the church was constructed in 1844 and 
that defined York Mills through the early- to mid-twentieth century. Nonetheless, the 
church and its larger property have maintained their integrity as representative of 
nineteenth-century ecclesiastical architecture and landscapes, while adapting to the 
evolving patterns of land use within York Mills. Changes to the church property to adapt 
to the evolving context include the closure of the carriageway from Yonge Street; the 
construction of a pedestrian pathway from Yonge to the church; the construction of the 
parking lot on the north side of the property; and extensive landscaping situating the 
church and the property within a mature, treed environment which is celebrated today 
as an oasis and landscape of reflection. 
The construction of the contemporary office park located at 4025 Yonge Street (York 
Mills Centre) on the northeast corner of Yonge Street and York Mills Road, in tandem 
with the growth of trees along the slope of the ridge behind, has largely impeded the 
historic view of St. John’s York Mills Anglican Church from Yonge Street. The only 
visible indication of its presence on Yonge Street is the Kay Gate immediately to the 
south of the C.W. Jefferys House at 4111 Yonge Street. From Old Yonge Street, the 
Dawson Lychgate demarcates the entrance to the churchyard and the church beyond. 
The primary means of access by vehicle is a driveway located on Don Ridge Drive, a 
dead-end street and cul-de-sac that runs west off Old Yonge Street. 
The evolved post-war suburban landscape has erased most of York Mills rural 
character; however, several properties that share a similar period of construction with 
St. John’s York Mills Anglican Church remain and collectively relay the history of the 
community. These include: 
• 4111 Yonge Street, C.W. Jefferys House (1833, designated Part IV) 
• 4150 Yonge Street, John Street Worker’s Cottages (1860, listed) 
• 174 Old Yonge Street, St John’s Rectory (1878, designated Part IV) 
19 Don Ridge Drive - Notice of Intention to Designate Page 22 of 33

• 106 York Mills Road, York Mills Baptist Church Manse (1850, listed) 
• 3885 Yonge Street, Jolly Miller Tavern (1857, designated Part IV) 
Collectively, and alongside the remaining natural features including the ridge and 
western branch of the Don River, these properties convey the history of colonial 
settlement and religious practice within York Mills through the nineteenth and into the 
twentieth centuries and are valued by the present-day community of York Mills and 
North York.
